why.heading: Every frame is *a decision*
paragraphs: The audience never lie. They just leave.
At my first screening, I watched people check their phones during a scene I loved. Nobody said a word. They didn't have to. That scene was gone in the next cut.
Made me realise users do the same thing. They don't complain, they just leave. So I watch what they do. It tells me where they get stuck and what to fix first, in a film or a product.
why.quote: “I storyboard features before I build them, and I edit roadmaps the way I edit a film.”

caseStudies.heading: Product calls, *worked end to end*
caseStudies.sub: Each one starts with a real problem someone has, picks one number that would prove the fix worked, and ends with something you can actually click.

items.title: Day Zero for Groww

rows.label: Problem
rows.text: You finish KYC on Groww, you’re excited to invest, and then you wait up to a day with nothing to do. That’s exactly when people lose interest.

rows.label: Solution
rows.text: Let people plan their first investment while the account is being activated. When it goes live, they confirm it in one tap.

rows.label: Guardrails
rows.text: No recommendations, nothing runs on its own, and no F&O or margin. It should help people start, not push them.

items.metricText: The number I’d watch: how many newly activated users invest within 72 hours, tested 50/50 against the current flow

items.title: Investly: from signup to first investment

rows.label: Question
rows.text: Where do people drop off between signing up and their first mutual fund investment, and what should the team test next?

rows.label: Found
rows.text: Only ==9.0%== of signups ever invested. The biggest leak is between looking at a fund and starting to invest (35.5%), and 31% of people who started never finished.

rows.label: Recommended
rows.text: Nudge people in their first week, recover failed checkouts, A/B test SIP projections, and move spend to referrals, which bring in investors at ₹849 each.

items.title: ShotList: from scene to shoot day

rows.label: Problem
rows.text: Student filmmakers lose days turning a script into a shot list, a call sheet and a budget. Most just skip it, and then the shoot day falls apart.

rows.label: Solution
rows.text: Paste a scene and get a shot list, a call sheet and a rough budget in a minute. You edit it, export it, and you’re ready to shoot.

rows.label: Who uses it
rows.text: Built for and tested with members of Bioscope, VIT-AP’s film club.

items.metricText: The one number I track: weekly active filmmakers, meaning how many come back and use it every week

items.kind: AI · Agentic commerce · Razorpay AI Buildathon
items.title: Kirana Shop
items.summary: A shop owner photographs his shelf, and his shop becomes searchable and buyable by an AI agent. No money moves until he confirms the item is in stock.
items.metricText: from shelf photos to an AI-buyable catalogue

details.label: Problem
details.text: You can ask an AI assistant to order biscuits from Blinkit. You can’t ask it to order from the kirana shop down your street. UPI already works there. The problem is that the shop’s stock doesn’t exist anywhere a computer can read.

details.label: Approach
details.text: Shelf photos go to Gemini vision, which writes the catalogue. A buyer asks in plain language and the agent resolves it against the catalogue, handling brands, misspellings and plurals. Before any payment, the owner confirms the item is actually on the shelf.

details.label: Outcome
details.text: A working prototype for Track 01 (AI Growth & Agentic Commerce): discovery, cataloguing and owner-approved payments, with an append-only audit log and 35 test inputs run through the full flow.

details.label: What I did
details.text: Worked out why nobody had solved this yet (Razorpay has the payments, Google knows where the shop is, nobody knows what’s on the shelf), designed the flow, built it, and fixed a nasty bug where the agent said “we don’t have it” and then suggested the very same item.

items.title: Rapido Trip Chaining
items.summary: Book a train ticket in Rapido, and the ride to the station is offered in the same flow, timed to reach 20 minutes before departure. Even when the ticket is for someone else.

details.label: Problem
details.text: Booking a train and getting to the station are two separate jobs today, so the ride gets planned at the last minute, often in another app. When the ticket is for a parent, nobody arranges their ride at all.

details.label: Approach
details.text: Once the ticket is confirmed, Rapido proposes a bike pickup timed to the departure. If the ticket is for someone else, it asks for their pickup address instead of assuming it, and texts the captain’s details to them directly. Both legs then sit together as one trip in My Rides.

details.label: Outcome
details.text: A working prototype covering review and pay, ticket confirmation, the chained pickup for yourself or someone else, and the multi-leg trip view, with a guided “watch it work” mode.

details.label: What I did
details.text: Noticed the gap between booking a ticket and actually getting to the station, designed the flow (including the case where you’re booking for your mom), and built the prototype.

items.title: Funnel & Retention Analysis
items.summary: The view → cart → purchase funnel, weekly retention cohorts and price-tier segments, built on real store data.

details.label: Problem
details.text: Product teams need to know where users drop off, how well new users come back, and which segments matter, often before they have a production analytics setup.

details.label: Approach
details.text: Loaded 885,129 real events (view, cart, purchase) from a public electronics-store dataset covering five months, then used SQL in DuckDB to build the funnel, weekly retention cohorts, a 7-day activation rate and price-tier segments.

details.label: Outcome
details.text: View to cart 9.08%, cart to purchase 57.65%, 7-day activation 5.00%. Weekly cohorts of 7,700–21,000 new users fall to 400–600 by week 1. Premium items sell almost as often as mid-priced ones at about 6× the order value.

details.label: What I did
details.text: Picked the questions, wrote the SQL and Python, made the charts, and boiled it all down to one call: fix onboarding and the first week before anything else.

items.title: Feedback Intelligence
items.summary: Turns messy Play Store reviews for Swiggy and PhonePe into a ranked, developer-ready list of what to fix first.
items.metricText: reviews → 25 issues · 122.5× error spike behind the top one

details.label: Problem
details.text: Feedback is scattered across reviews and tickets, with no systematic way to separate signal from noise or connect it to what is actually breaking in production.

details.label: Approach
details.text: Scraped 1,600 real reviews, classified them with an LLM, clustered duplicates with TF-IDF and K-Means, checked each cluster against backend error data (synthetic), and ranked issues with a transparent weighted score.

details.label: Outcome
details.text: About 300 actionable reviews collapsed into 25 issues. Payment-fraud and duplicate-charge complaints matched a 122.5× spike in payment errors, the top priority, followed by checkout refunds at 93×.

details.label: What I did
details.text: Built the whole pipeline and a scoring formula anyone can follow, so every priority has a clear reason behind it. It also writes up issue reports for the top five.

exploring.heading: Questions I'm *thinking about*
exploring.sub: Open product questions I keep coming back to. Two come straight from the world I know best: the movies.

items.question: Why do viewers abandon a film in its first ten minutes on OTT, and what should a platform measure instead of views?
items.why: Views reward the click, not the film. A better North Star could change what gets made and recommended.

items.question: How could BookMyShow bring people back to theatres for mid-budget films?
items.why: Big releases still fill halls while mid-budget films wait for OTT. That gap is a demand problem, and product can move it.

items.question: Can a ₹200 quick-commerce basket ever make money?
items.why: Ten-minute delivery is loved and expensive. I want to find the order size, batching and density where it pays for itself.

items.question: What should the North Star be for an AI speaking coach, and what kills activation in week one?
items.why: People download language apps feeling brave and quit the first time they feel judged. Activation is an emotional problem as much as a funnel.

film.heading: The other *half of me*
film.intro: When I’m not working on products, I’m making films with FrameFlash Productions, my own studio, or running Bioscope, VIT-AP’s film club. Honestly, making a film is product work with a camera: a small team, a tight budget, a hard deadline, and an audience that decides in seconds whether it cares.

bridge.title: Audience *first*
bridge.text: A film fails when the audience stops caring. A product fails when the user does.

bridge.title: Storyboard = *prototype*
bridge.text: I plan every shot before the camera rolls, the way I prototype before anything gets built.

bridge.title: The edit = *prioritisation*
bridge.text: Cutting a good scene to make a better film is the same call as cutting a good feature to ship a better product.
